title: Variables, Types, and Collections
summary: Declare it right, know its type, and shape your data: let and const, coercion, truthy and falsy, arrays, Map and Set, and JSON.

lessons.title: var, let and const
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, write code to create variables and initialize them correctly.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: A **variable** is a name that holds a value. JavaScript gives you three ways to make one: `var`, `let` and `const`. They differ in where the name works, called its **scope**. They also differ in whether you can reassign them, and in what happens if you read them too early.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: Name tags on boxes. A `const` tag is glued to one box for good, but you can still change what is inside the box. A `let` tag can move to another box. Where it stops: a `var` tag ignores room walls, so it wanders out of `if` and `for` blocks.

cards.title: Block or function?
cards.body: `let` and `const` are **block-scoped**: they live only inside the nearest `{ }`. `var` is **function-scoped**: it ignores `if` and `for` blocks and lives in the whole function. Outside any function, it lives in the whole script.

cards.title: Reading too early
cards.body: `var` declarations are **hoisted**: set up before any code runs, holding `undefined`. `let` and `const` wait in the **temporal dead zone** (TDZ) until their line runs. Reading them earlier throws.

cards.title: const locks the name, not the object
cards.code:
const user = { name: 'Ana' };
user.name = 'Bo'; // fine
user.age = 30;    // fine
user = {};        // TypeError
cards.body: `const` must get a value right away and can never be **reassigned**. The object it points to can still change.

cards.title: More rules
items: Declaring the same `let` or `const` twice in one scope is a `SyntaxError`. `var` allows it.
`const rate;` with no value is a `SyntaxError`.
Assigning to a name you never declared creates a **global** variable in sloppy mode.
In **strict mode** (`'use strict'`), that same assignment throws a `ReferenceError`.

cards.body: "`const` makes an object read-only." Wrong. `const` only glues the name to one value. Properties can still be added, changed or deleted. To lock the object itself, use `Object.freeze()`.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **"const by default, let when it changes, var never."** Read too early: `var` says `undefined`, `let` and `const` throw.

terms.say: A name that holds a value, like a labeled box. You use the name to get the value back later.
The part of the code where a name can be used. Outside its scope, the name does not exist.
Lives only inside the nearest pair of curly braces. When the block ends, the name is gone.
Lives in the whole function it was made in, even outside the if or for block where you wrote it.
Set up before any code runs. A hoisted var already exists at the top, holding undefined, until its line gives it a value.
The time between the start of a block and the line that declares a let or const. Touching the name then throws an error.
Pointed at a new value with =. A const can never be reassigned. A let can.
A variable every part of the program can see. Making one by accident is a classic bug.
A stricter set of JavaScript rules, switched on with 'use strict'. Mistakes that used to pass quietly now throw errors.
Locks an object so nobody can add, change or delete its properties. Changes are ignored, or throw in strict mode.

lessons.title: Primitive types and typeof
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, write code to create variables and initialize them correctly.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Every value has a type. There are seven **primitive** types: string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, symbol and null. Everything else is an **object**, including arrays and functions. The `typeof` operator tells you the type as a string, like `'number'`.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: Primitives are coins: a 5 is a 5, and you can't reshape a coin. Objects are backpacks: you can put things in and take them out. Where it stops: coins come with a free helper, so `'hi'.toUpperCase()` still works on a plain string.

cards.title: Primitives never change
cards.body: Primitives are **immutable**. No method changes them in place: `s.toUpperCase()` returns a new string and `s` stays the same. Methods work because JavaScript briefly wraps the value in a **wrapper object** (`String`, `Number`, `Boolean`…). `null` and `undefined` have no wrapper, so `null.x` throws a `TypeError`.

cards.title: What typeof says
cards.code:
typeof 'hi'          // 'string'
typeof 42            // 'number'
typeof 10n           // 'bigint'
typeof undefined     // 'undefined'
typeof Symbol()      // 'symbol'
typeof null          // 'object' (old bug)
typeof []            // 'object'
typeof function(){}  // 'function'
cards.body: `typeof` always returns a string. Functions and classes give `'function'`, even though they are objects.

cards.title: Check arrays and null the right way
cards.body: `typeof []` is `'object'`, so use `Array.isArray(value)`. To find `null`, compare directly: `value === null`. `typeof` on a name that was never declared returns `'undefined'`, with no error. But `typeof` on a `let` or `const` before its line throws.

cards.title: undefined vs null
cards.body: `undefined` means "no value yet". You get it from a declared variable with no value, a missing property, or a function with no `return`. `null` means "empty on purpose". Your code sets it, and some built-ins return it, like `match()` when nothing matches.
"`typeof null` is `'null'`." Wrong. It is `'object'`, a bug kept since the first version of JavaScript. Also: `typeof NaN` is `'number'`.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **"Seven coins, then backpacks."** String, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, symbol, null. Everything else is an object.

terms.say: A simple, single value like a number or a piece of text. It is not an object and it can never be changed in place.
A container that holds named values. Arrays, functions and dates are all objects.
An operator that tells you a value's type as a word, like 'string' or 'number'.
Can never be changed. To get a different value, you make a new one.
A helper object JavaScript makes for a moment around a primitive, so you can call methods like toUpperCase on it.
Gives true only for real arrays. Use it because typeof says object for arrays.
A value that means "empty on purpose". Code uses it to show there is nothing there.
The value of something that has no value yet, like a variable you declared but never set.
The error you get when you use a value the wrong way, like reading a property of null.

lessons.title: Strings and template literals
lessons.objective: Given a business requirement, utilize strings, numbers, and dates effectively.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: A **string** is text. You can write it in single quotes, double quotes or backticks. Backticks make a **template literal**: text with `${...}` holes for values, and real line breaks. Strings are **immutable**, so every string method returns a new string.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A template literal is a fill-in-the-blanks form. You write the sentence once and leave holes. JavaScript fills each hole when the line runs. Where it stops: a hole takes any expression, like a sum or a function call, not just a name.

cards.title: Fill the holes
cards.body: Each `${...}` runs its expression and drops the result into the text. In plain quotes, the same characters would print as they are.

cards.title: slice vs substring
cards.body: `slice(start, end)` copies from `start` up to, but not including, `end`. Negative numbers count from the end: `'hello'.slice(-3)` is `'llo'`. `substring` treats negatives as 0. It also swaps its two numbers when start is bigger than end.

cards.title: replace vs replaceAll
cards.body: `replace` with a string pattern changes only the **first match**. `replaceAll` changes every match. With a **regular expression** (regex), `replace` needs the `g` flag to change them all. `replaceAll` with a regex that lacks `g` throws a `TypeError`.

cards.title: Everyday tools
items: `split(',')` makes an array; `join(',')` makes a string
`indexOf` gives a position, or `-1` when missing

cards.body: "`s.replace('a', 'b')` swaps every `a`." Wrong. With a string pattern, only the first one changes. Use `replaceAll`, or a regex with the `g` flag.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **"Backticks bake in values."** And string methods never change the old string, so keep the result: `s = s.trim()`.

terms.say: A piece of text, like a word or a sentence, wrapped in quotes or backticks.
Text written between backticks. It can hold holes with values in them, and it can span many lines.
Can never be changed. String methods give you a new string and leave the old one alone.
Copies part of a string. Negative numbers count back from the end.
Copies part of a string, like slice. But it treats negative numbers as 0 and swaps the numbers if they are backwards.
Only the first place the pattern shows up. Later copies are left alone.
Changes every place a pattern shows up in a string, not just the first one.
A pattern for finding text, written between slashes, like /cat/g. The g at the end means "find them all".
Removes spaces, tabs and line breaks from both ends of a string.
Cuts a string into an array of pieces at each comma. The pieces don't include the commas.

lessons.title: Numbers, Math, BigInt and dates
lessons.objective: Given a business requirement, utilize strings, numbers, and dates effectively.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: JavaScript has one main **number** type for whole numbers and decimals alike. It stores them as **floating point** values, so some decimals come out slightly off. For huge whole numbers there is **BigInt**. Dates and times live in `Date` objects.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A ruler with very fine marks. Most values land right on a mark. Some, like 0.1, fall between two marks and get rounded to the nearest one. Where it stops: whole numbers are exact up to 2^53 − 1; past that, the marks get too far apart.

cards.title: NaN is odd
cards.code:
NaN === NaN;          // false
Number.isNaN(NaN);    // true
isNaN('abc');         // true  (converts first)
Number.isNaN('abc');  // false (no converting)
0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3;    // false
cards.body: `NaN` means **not a number**. It is the only value not equal to itself, so test it with `Number.isNaN()`.

cards.title: Numbers from text
cards.body: `parseInt('42px', 10)` reads the leading digits and stops at the first letter: `42`. Always pass the **radix**, the number base (usually 10). `Number('42px')` is stricter and gives `NaN`. `parseFloat('3.5kg')` gives `3.5`.

cards.title: Rounding
cards.body: `toFixed(2)` rounds to 2 decimals and returns a **string**: `(1.5).toFixed(2)` is `'1.50'`. `Math.round`, `Math.floor`, `Math.ceil` and `Math.max` return numbers. `Math.random()` gives a number from 0 up to, but not including, 1.

cards.title: BigInt
cards.body: `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` is 9007199254740991 (2^53 − 1). Past it, whole numbers lose precision. A BigInt like `10n` stays exact at any size. You can't mix BigInt and number in math: `10n + 1` throws a `TypeError`. `Math` methods don't take BigInts either.

cards.title: Dates
cards.body: `new Date(2022, 0, 31)` is 31 January 2022. Months are **zero-based** (January is 0); days start at 1. `getMonth()` returns 0 to 11. Parts that are too big roll over: day 32 of January is 1 February. `Date.now()` gives milliseconds since 1 January 1970 UTC. To show a date to people, use `toLocaleDateString()` or `Intl.DateTimeFormat`.
"`getMonth()` on a March date returns 3." Wrong. It returns 2, because January is 0. The day of the month, `getDate()`, starts at 1.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **"NaN won't even match itself."** And months start at zero, days at one.

terms.say: The JavaScript type for both whole numbers and decimals, like 7 or 2.5.
The way computers store decimals. Some decimals, like 0.1, can only be stored very close, not exactly.
A type for whole numbers of any size. You write it with an n at the end, like 10n. It is always exact.
NaN is a special number value that means "this math failed", like 0 divided by 0. It is not even equal to itself.
Gives true only if the value really is NaN. It does not convert text first, unlike the older isNaN().
The number base to read digits in. Base 10 is normal counting. Pass it to parseInt so nothing gets guessed.
Reads the whole number at the start of a text and stops at the first character that is not a digit.
Counting starts at 0, not 1. For Date months, January is 0 and December is 11.
Gives the current time as the number of milliseconds since the start of 1970, in UTC.

lessons.title: Type coercion: +, - and == vs ===
lessons.objective: Given a scenario or example, demonstrate awareness of type coercion and its effects.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: **Type coercion** is JavaScript changing a value's type by itself so an operation can work. It happens with `+`, `-`, `==` and more. It is sometimes handy, but it causes most "why did that print?" bugs.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A translator. You hand over two things in different languages, and they turn both into one language before working. Where it stops: this translator follows fixed rules, so once you know the rules, every result is predictable.

cards.title: + loves strings
cards.body: `+` first turns both sides into **primitives**. If either side is then a string, it joins them: `1 + '2'` is `'12'`, and `[] + {}` is `'[object Object]'`. Otherwise it adds numbers: `true + 1` is `2`. It works left to right: `1 + 2 + '3'` is `'33'`.

cards.title: - * / want numbers
cards.body: `-`, `*` and `/` always convert to numbers. `'5' - 2` is `3`, and `'5' * '2'` is `10`. Text that isn't a number becomes `NaN`. Objects become strings first, then numbers: `[] - 1` is `-1`, because `[]` becomes `''`, then `0`.

cards.title: == vs ===
cards.code:
1 == '1'             // true  (converts)
1 === '1'            // false (no converting)
null == undefined    // true
null == 0            // false
null >= 0            // true
Object.is(NaN, NaN)  // true
cards.body: **Loose equality** (`==`) converts types first. **Strict equality** (`===`) never converts. `Object.is` works like `===`, except `NaN` equals `NaN` and `0` differs from `-0`.

cards.title: Convert on purpose
items: `+'7'` gives `7`: the **unary plus** turns a value into a number

cards.body: "`null == 0` is true, since `null` is like zero." Wrong. `==` has a special rule: `null` only equals `undefined` (and itself). Yet `null >= 0` is `true`, because `>=` does convert `null` to `0`.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **"Plus picks text, minus picks math."** And use `===` unless you really want the conversion.

terms.say: JavaScript changing a value from one type to another by itself, like turning the number 1 into the text "1".
Simple single values, like numbers, strings and booleans. They are not objects.
A special number value that means "this math failed". It is not equal to anything, not even itself.
Comparing with ==. JavaScript converts the two values to a shared type before comparing them.
Comparing with ===. The values must have the same type and the same value. Nothing is converted.
A way to check if two values are the same. It is like ===, but it says NaN is NaN and keeps 0 and -0 apart.
A + with only one value after it, like +"7". It turns the value into a number.
The text you get when a plain object is turned into a string. It is the default, and it is rarely what you want.

lessons.title: Truthy, falsy and the logical operators
lessons.objective: Given a specific scenario, distinguish truthy or falsey evaluations.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: When JavaScript needs a yes or no, in an `if`, a loop or after `!`, it turns any value into `true` or `false`. Values that become `false` are **falsy**. All the others are **truthy**.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A door with a short "no entry" list. Only eight values are turned away; those are falsy. Everyone else walks in, even values that look empty, like `[]` or `'0'`. Where it stops: truthy does not mean `== true`. That is a different rule.

cards.title: Everything else is truthy
cards.body: That includes `[]`, `{}`, `'0'`, `'false'`, a string with one space, and `new Boolean(false)`. Any object is truthy, even an empty one. To check for an empty array, test `arr.length`.

cards.title: || and && hand back values
cards.body: `a || b` returns the first truthy **operand**, or the last one. `a && b` returns the first falsy operand, or the last one. They return the value itself, not a **boolean**. Both **short-circuit**: they stop as soon as the answer is known.

cards.title: ?? and ?.
cards.body: **Nullish coalescing** (`??`) falls back only for `null` or `undefined`, so a real `0` survives. **Optional chaining** (`?.`) stops at `null` or `undefined` and gives `undefined`.

cards.title: Assign only when needed
cards.body: `a ||= b` sets `a` only if `a` is falsy. `a &&= b` sets it only if `a` is truthy. `a ??= b` sets it only if `a` is `null` or `undefined`. Write `!!value` to get a real `true` or `false`.
"`[]` is empty, so `if ([])` is skipped." Wrong. Every object is truthy, even an empty array. Check `arr.length` instead.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **"Eight say no."** false, 0, -0, 0n, empty string, null, undefined, NaN. Use `??` when 0 is a real answer.

terms.say: A value that counts as "no" in an if. There are only eight, like 0, empty text, null and undefined.
A value that counts as "yes" in an if. Every value that is not falsy is truthy, even an empty array.
An old browser object kept for very old web pages. It is the one object that counts as falsy.
An object that wraps the value false. Because it is an object, it counts as truthy. Avoid it.
A value an operator works on. In a || b, both a and b are operands.
A value that is either true or false, nothing else.
Stop early. Once the answer is clear, the right side is never even run.
The ?? operator. It uses the right side only when the left side is null or undefined. A 0 or empty text is kept.
The ?. operator. If the value on its left is null or undefined, it stops and gives undefined instead of an error.

lessons.title: Arrays: change it or copy it?
lessons.objective: Given a list of data, demonstrate data manipulation with arrays.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: An **array** is an ordered list, like `['a', 'b', 'c']`. Positions, called **indexes**, start at 0. Some array methods **mutate**: they change the array itself. Others hand back a new array and leave the original alone. The exam loves asking which is which.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: Mutating is writing on the original page. Copying is making a photocopy first and writing on the copy. Where it stops: array copies are **shallow**. Objects inside are shared, not photocopied.

cards.title: These change the array
items: `push` / `pop`: add or remove at the end
`unshift` / `shift`: add or remove at the start

cards.title: These give you something new
items: `slice(start, end)`: a copy of a part
`concat`: joins arrays into a new one
`Array.from(x)`: an array from any iterable or array-like value, like a string or a `Set`

cards.title: slice copies, splice cuts
cards.body: `slice` copies. `splice` cuts items out of the original and returns the removed ones.

cards.title: Finding things
cards.body: `includes(x)` gives `true` or `false` and can find `NaN`. `indexOf(x)` gives the position, or `-1`. It uses `===`, so it never finds `NaN`. `at(-1)` reads the last item (new in ES2022); `arr[arr.length - 1]` works everywhere.
"`const sorted = arr.sort()` keeps `arr` safe." Wrong. `sort` reorders `arr` in place and returns that same array. Copy first: `[...arr].sort()`. Also, `push` returns the new length, not the array.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **"Splice is surgery, slice is a photocopy."** Surgery changes the patient.

terms.say: A list of values kept in order. Each value sits at a numbered spot, starting at 0.
The numbered spots in an array. The first spot is index 0, the second is index 1.
Change the thing itself, instead of making a changed copy.
A copy of only the outer list. Objects inside are shared, so changing one shows up in both lists.
Cuts items out of an array, and can put new ones in, right in the original. It returns what it cut out.
Copies part of an array into a new one. The original stays the same.
The ... syntax. It spills out every item of a list, so [...arr] makes a new array with the same items.
Builds a new array from anything you can loop over, like a string or a Set, or from an array-like value.
Tells you true or false: is this value in the array? It can even find NaN.
Tells you where a value sits in an array, or -1 if it is not there. It can never find NaN.

lessons.title: Arrays: map, filter, reduce, find and sort
lessons.objective: Given a list of data, demonstrate data manipulation with arrays.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Most array work is "do something with each item". Array methods do the looping for you. Each one takes a **callback**: a function you pass in, which runs once per item. Pick the method by what you want back.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A factory belt. `map` repaints every box. `filter` lets only some boxes through. `reduce` packs every box into one crate. `find` grabs the first box that fits. Where it stops: `forEach` just walks the belt and hands back nothing.

cards.title: What each one returns
items: `filter`: a new array of the items that pass

cards.title: reduce
cards.code:
const cart = [{ price: 5 }, { price: 7 }];
cart.reduce((sum, item) => sum + item.price, 0); // 12

[].reduce((a, b) => a + b);    // TypeError
[].reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0); // 0
cards.body: `reduce` carries an **accumulator**, the running result, from item to item. Always give it a start value. On an empty array with no start value, it throws a `TypeError`.

cards.title: sort
cards.body: By default `sort` compares items as strings, so `'10'` comes before `'2'`. For numbers, pass a **compare function**. A negative result puts `a` first.

cards.title: forEach can't stop
cards.body: There is no `break` in `forEach`, and a `return` only ends that one callback. To stop early, use a `for...of` loop. Or use `some`, `every`, `find` or `findIndex`, which stop by themselves once they know the answer.
"`map` without `return` keeps the items." Wrong. A callback with braces and no `return` returns `undefined`, so you get an array of `undefined`. Write `n => n * 2`, or add `return`.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **"Map makes, filter keeps, reduce squeezes."** Sort numbers with `(a, b) => a - b`.

terms.say: A function you hand to another function, so it can call yours later, here once for each item.
Makes a new array by running your function on every item. Same number of items out as in.
Makes a new array with only the items your function says yes to.
Walks through the array and squeezes all the items into one single value, like a total.
Gives the first item your function says yes to, or undefined if none match.
Runs your function once for each item. It gives back nothing, and break can't stop it.
The running result that reduce carries from one item to the next, like a running total.
A function you give to sort. It gets two items and returns a negative number, zero or a positive number to say which goes first.
A loop that walks through each item of an array or other list. You can stop it with break.
Tells you true if at least one item passes your test. It stops at the first one that does.

lessons.title: Map, Set and WeakMap
lessons.objective: Given a list of data, demonstrate data manipulation with arrays.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Besides objects and arrays, JavaScript has **collections** built for one job. A **Map** stores key-value pairs, and any value can be a key. A **Set** stores values with no repeats. A **WeakMap** attaches data to objects without keeping those objects alive.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A Map is a coat check: you hand over any item and it keeps a ticket for it. A Set is a guest book that refuses to write the same name twice. Where it stops: two look-alike objects are still two different guests.

cards.title: Map
cards.body: Keys can be objects, functions, anything. A Map remembers **insertion order**, and `size` is a property, not a method.

cards.title: Map or plain object?
cards.body: Object keys are always strings or symbols: the number `1` becomes `'1'`. A Map keeps the real key. A Map is easy to loop with `for...of`, and its size is ready to read. Plain objects are still best for fixed shapes and for JSON.

cards.title: Set
cards.body: `new Set(array)` drops repeats. Spread it back into an array to **de-duplicate**. Set has `add`, `has`, `delete` and `size`.

cards.title: WeakMap and WeakSet
cards.body: WeakMap keys must be objects (newer engines also allow some symbols). It holds them **weakly**: once nothing else uses a key object, the **garbage collector** can delete it and its entry. So a WeakMap has no `size` and can't be looped over. **WeakSet** works the same way for values.
"`map.size()` returns the count." Wrong. `size` is a property: `map.size`. And `map['key'] = 1` doesn't add an entry. Use `set` to add and `get` to read.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **"Map maps anything, Set says it once, WeakMap lets go."**

terms.say: Containers that hold many values, like arrays, Maps and Sets.
A list of key and value pairs. Any value can be a key, even an object, and it remembers the order you added them.
A list where every value can appear only once. Adding the same value again does nothing.
Like a Map, but its keys must be objects, and it lets go of an entry when nothing else uses that key object.
The order you added things in. A Map gives its entries back in that same order.
A property that tells how many entries a Map or Set has. You read it without parentheses.
Remove the repeats, so each value is left only once.
Without keeping it alive. If nothing else needs the object, it can be cleaned away.
The part of JavaScript that frees memory by deleting values nothing can reach anymore.
Like a Set, but it holds only objects, lets go of them when nothing else uses them, and can't be looped over.

lessons.title: JSON in and out
lessons.objective: Given a JSON response, demonstrate how to operate the JSON object.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: **JSON** (JavaScript Object Notation) is a text format for sending data, for example in an API response. It looks like a JavaScript object, but it is just a string. `JSON.parse` turns JSON text into values. `JSON.stringify` turns values into JSON text.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: Flat-pack furniture. `stringify` packs an object into a box of text you can ship. `parse` unpacks it into a real object again. Where it stops: some parts never fit in the box, like functions and `undefined`. And a `Date` comes out as plain text.

cards.title: JSON rules are strict
cards.body: Keys need **double quotes**: `{"id": 1}`. Strings use double quotes too. No **trailing commas**, no comments, no `undefined`, no functions. `JSON.parse` on invalid text throws a `SyntaxError`. So wrap it in `try...catch` when the text comes from outside.

cards.title: What stringify drops
cards.body: In objects, `undefined`, functions and symbols are **left out**. In arrays they become `null`. A BigInt throws.

cards.title: Pick keys and indent
cards.body: The second argument is a **replacer**: an array of keys to keep, or a function. The third adds indentation for humans.

cards.title: Dates and toJSON
cards.body: If an object has a `toJSON()` method, `stringify` uses whatever it returns. `Date` has one, so a date becomes an **ISO string** like `"2022-06-01T00:00:00.000Z"`. `parse` gives back that string, not a `Date`. A **reviver**, the second argument of `parse`, can turn it back.
"`JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj))` makes a perfect copy." Not always. It drops `undefined` and functions, turns dates into strings, and throws on BigInt. It is fine for plain data only.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **"Stringify packs, parse unpacks."** Double quotes always; functions never make the trip.

terms.say: A plain text way to write data, like {"id": 1}. Programs use it to send data to each other.
Reads JSON text and builds real values from it, like objects, arrays and numbers.
Turns values like objects and arrays into JSON text, so you can send or save them.
The " marks. JSON only accepts these around keys and strings, never single quotes.
A comma after the last item in a list or object. JavaScript allows it, but JSON does not.

flashcards.front: What is the scope of `let`, `const` and `var`?
flashcards.back: `let` and `const` are block-scoped: they live inside the nearest `{ }`. `var` is function-scoped: it lives in the whole function, or the whole script.

flashcards.front: What happens if you read a variable before its declaration line?
flashcards.back: `var` gives `undefined`, because it is hoisted with that value. `let` and `const` throw a `ReferenceError`: they are in the temporal dead zone.

flashcards.front: Can you change an object stored in a `const`?
flashcards.back: Yes. `const` only stops reassigning the name. You can still add, change or delete properties. Use `Object.freeze()` to lock the object.

flashcards.front: What happens when you assign to a name you never declared?
flashcards.back: In sloppy mode it quietly creates a global variable. In strict mode it throws a `ReferenceError`.

flashcards.front: What are the seven primitive types?
flashcards.back: string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, symbol and null. Everything else is an object, including arrays and functions.

flashcards.front: What does `typeof null` return?
flashcards.back: `'object'`. It is a bug from the first version of JavaScript. Check for null with `value === null`.

flashcards.front: How do you check whether a value is an array?
flashcards.back: Use `Array.isArray(value)`. `typeof` returns `'object'` for arrays, so it can't tell them from plain objects.

flashcards.front: What can a template literal do that quotes can't?
flashcards.back: Template literals use backticks. They can hold `${expression}` holes that are filled with values, and they can contain real line breaks.

flashcards.front: How do `slice` and `substring` treat negative numbers?
flashcards.back: `slice` counts negatives back from the end. `substring` treats negatives as 0, and swaps its two numbers if start is bigger than end.

flashcards.front: Does `'a-b-c'.replace('-', '+')` change every dash?
flashcards.back: No. With a string pattern, `replace` changes only the first match, giving `'a+b-c'`. Use `replaceAll` or a regex with the `g` flag.

flashcards.front: How do you test whether a value is `NaN`?
flashcards.back: Use `Number.isNaN(x)`. `NaN === NaN` is always false. Global `isNaN()` converts first, so `isNaN('abc')` is true, but `Number.isNaN('abc')` is false.

flashcards.front: What type does `toFixed()` return?
flashcards.back: A string, rounded to that many decimals. `(1.5).toFixed(2)` is `'1.50'`. Adding to it joins text instead of adding numbers.

flashcards.front: When do you need BigInt?
flashcards.back: For whole numbers past `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` (2^53 − 1). Write `10n`. You can't mix BigInt with number in math; that throws a `TypeError`.

flashcards.front: What does `getMonth()` return for a date in January?
flashcards.back: `0`. Date months are zero-based, from 0 to 11. Days of the month, from `getDate()`, start at 1.

flashcards.front: What is `1 + '2'`, and what is `'5' - 2`?
flashcards.back: `1 + '2'` is `'12'`: `+` joins when either side is a string. `'5' - 2` is `3`: `-` always converts to numbers.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between `==` and `===`?
flashcards.back: `==` converts the values to a shared type before comparing. `===` never converts: type and value must both match. Prefer `===`.

flashcards.front: Is `null == 0` true?
flashcards.back: No. With `==`, `null` only equals `undefined` and itself. But `null >= 0` is `true`, because `>=` converts `null` to `0`.

flashcards.front: How is `Object.is` different from `===`?
flashcards.back: `Object.is(NaN, NaN)` is `true` and `Object.is(0, -0)` is `false`. For every other pair it agrees with `===`.

flashcards.front: Which values are falsy?
flashcards.back: `false`, `0`, `-0`, `0n`, `''`, `null`, `undefined` and `NaN` (plus `document.all` in browsers). Everything else is truthy, including `[]`, `{}` and `'0'`.

flashcards.front: What do `||` and `&&` return?
flashcards.back: A value, not always a boolean. `||` returns the first truthy operand, or the last one. `&&` returns the first falsy operand, or the last one.

flashcards.front: When should you use `??` instead of `||`?
flashcards.back: When `0` or `''` are valid values. `??` falls back only for `null` or `undefined`. So `0 ?? 5` is `0`, but `0 || 5` is `5`.

flashcards.front: Which array methods change the original array?
flashcards.back: `push`, `pop`, `shift`, `unshift`, `splice`, `sort`, `reverse` and `fill`. `slice`, `concat`, `map`, `filter` and spread make new arrays.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between `slice` and `splice`?
flashcards.back: `slice(start, end)` copies a part into a new array; the original is unchanged. `splice(start, count)` removes items from the original and returns them.

flashcards.front: Why can `includes` find `NaN` but `indexOf` can't?
flashcards.back: `indexOf` compares with `===`, and `NaN === NaN` is false. `includes` uses SameValueZero, which treats `NaN` as equal to itself.

flashcards.front: How do you sort a copy and keep the original?
flashcards.back: Copy first, then sort: `[...arr].sort()` or `arr.slice().sort()`. `sort` itself changes the array in place.

flashcards.front: What do `map`, `filter` and `reduce` return?
flashcards.back: `map`: a new array of the same length. `filter`: a new array of the items that pass. `reduce`: one value built from all items.
By default, `sort` compares items as strings, and `'10'` comes before `'2'`. For numbers, pass `(a, b) => a - b`.

flashcards.front: When does `reduce` throw a `TypeError`?
flashcards.back: When the array is empty and you gave no start value. Pass a start value, like `0`, to be safe.

flashcards.front: How can you stop a loop over an array early?
flashcards.back: Not with `forEach`: it can't break. Use a `for...of` loop with `break`, or `some`, `every`, `find` or `findIndex`, which stop by themselves.

flashcards.front: When would you use a `Map` instead of a plain object?
flashcards.back: When keys are not strings, such as objects. Or when you need insertion order and an easy `size`. Object keys always become strings or symbols.

flashcards.front: How do you remove repeats from an array?
flashcards.back: `[...new Set(arr)]`. A `Set` keeps each value only once, and spread turns it back into an array.

flashcards.front: What makes a `WeakMap` different from a `Map`?
flashcards.back: Its keys must be objects, held weakly: an entry can vanish once its key object is unused elsewhere. It has no `size` and can't be looped over.

flashcards.front: What does `JSON.stringify` do with `undefined` and functions?
flashcards.back: In objects it leaves those keys out. In arrays it writes `null` in their place. A BigInt makes it throw a `TypeError`.

flashcards.front: What happens when `JSON.parse` gets invalid JSON?
flashcards.back: It throws a `SyntaxError`. Single-quoted keys, trailing commas and comments are all invalid. Wrap outside data in `try...catch`.

flashcards.front: Does a `Date` survive `JSON.stringify` and `JSON.parse`?
flashcards.back: No. `stringify` turns it into an ISO string through `toJSON()`. `parse` gives back that string. Use a reviver to rebuild the `Date`.

Month 5 is June, and the result is a string.
Month index 5 is June, since months are zero-based.

questions.code:
const user = { id: 1, name: 'Ana', password: 'x9' };
console.log(JSON.stringify(user, ['id', 'name']));
questions.explain: When the replacer is an array, only the listed keys are kept.
wrong: The array lists the keys to keep, not to drop.
The array is a replacer, not the value to convert.
Keys not in the replacer array are left out.

questions.explain: When a value has a `toJSON()` method, `stringify` uses what it returns. Here that is the string `$5`.
wrong: Methods are dropped, but `toJSON()` is called first.
`stringify` uses what `toJSON()` returns.
`toJSON()` returns the string `'$5'`.

questions.explain: `JSON.stringify` throws a `TypeError` on a BigInt value. You must convert it, for example with `toString()`, first.
wrong: BigInt values are not skipped like functions.
BigInt has no JSON form, so `stringify` throws.
BigInt is not turned into a string by itself.

questions.q: A developer wants to log `config` as JSON with a 2-space indent. Which call does it?
questions.explain: The third argument of `JSON.stringify` sets the indent. Pass `null` as the replacer to keep every key.
wrong: The second argument is the replacer; the indent is the third.
There is no options object; the indent is the third argument.
`parse` reads JSON; it doesn't write it.

questions.explain: The reviver turns only `price` into a number. `qty` stays the string `'2'`, so `+` joins: `'52'`.
wrong: `qty` is still the string `'2'`, so `+` joins.
No adding happens once a string is involved.
Joining a number and a string never gives `NaN`.

questions.q: A developer copies `data` with `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(data))`. Which two values will NOT come back the same? (Choose 2)
questions.explain: A date comes back as a string, and a method is dropped. Plain data like numbers, arrays, booleans and `null` round-trips fine.
wrong: Arrays of numbers fit JSON exactly.
`null` is valid JSON and comes back as `null`.
Booleans are valid JSON.

questions.explain: `stringify` works on any JSON value, not just objects. A string gets double quotes; `null` stays `null`.
wrong: JSON uses double quotes, and `null` is not quoted.
`null` is valid JSON, written as `null`.
A JSON string keeps its double quotes.
